notes:
# Research notes on Ezekiel 26 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How these notes were put together:** The verse-by-verse sources are mostly older or evangelical commentaries: Guzik (Enduring Word), Constable, Ellicott, Pulpit, Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), Keil & Delitzsch, Barnes, Clarke and Precept Austin. The Protestant traditions I found largely agree on this chapter. Where they differ, it's mostly about details: which month the prophecy came, whether "they" in v. 12 means Alexander, and what "never rebuilt" means. I found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. I also found nothing specifically Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox, so those are left out. Some pages I read in full have no citation markers, but each point still has its URL.

---

**v. 1 (the date)**
- **The month is missing in Hebrew.** Ellicott says the Hebrew gives the year Jerusalem fell but no month, and the month "cannot now be ascertained." He thinks the gap is probably a copying error. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **Why the BSB says "twelfth year, eleventh month."** A NET Bible note explains that dates normally include the month. According to D. I. Block (Ezekiel [NICOT], 2:34, n. 27) some emend to "in the twelfth year in the eleventh month" based partially on the copy of the LXX from Alexandrinus. The BSB wording seems to follow this kind of correction. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/verse.php?book=Eze&chapter=26&verse=14
- **Constable** mentions a related idea: the "eleventh month" may have dropped out because it matched the year number. Block reconstructed the date as February 3, 585 B.C., the date of the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar's 13-year siege of Tyre. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Older commentators guessed differently.**
  - Gill thinks the month was most likely the fifth, the first of which was twenty days after the taking it; in which time the news of it might be brought to Tyre. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/26-1.html
  - The Methodist writers Wesley and Benson say the same kind of thing. Wesley reads it as That month which followed the taking of Jerusalem. (same URL)
  - The Catholic Haydock commentary notes that Some think he speaks of the first, fourth, or fifth month. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Why the date matters.** JFB says giving a date at all, when the four nations before Tyre got none, marks the greater weight attached to the fall of Tyre. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 2 (Tyre's gloating)**
- **The sin was profiting from Jerusalem's fall.** Guzik says Tyre welcomed Jerusalem's ruin because it was good for trade, and calls her "blind with greed." He links the verse to Proverbs 17:5 and to God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/
- **The trade-route explanation.** Constable says Tyre controlled the sea routes and Judah the land routes, so Jerusalem's fall removed a competitor for toll money. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Was it greed alone, or religion too?** The commentators differ slightly here.
  - Ellicott says the gloating was of a purely selfish and commercial character, and shows nothing of the spitefulness and religious animosity of the nations mentioned in the previous chapter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-26.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary agrees that greed was the main motive. But it adds that The antagonism between their religion and the religion of the Jews would increase their joy at the downfall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/26.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch go further. They read Tyre as resenting Jerusalem's pull on the nations as the seat of the divine revelation of mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-2.htm
- **"Gate" is singular in meaning.** Ellicott explains that the Hebrew plural refers to the two leaves of one gate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **The Reformed Geneva Bible's lesson:** thus the wicked rejoice at their fall by whom they may have any profit or advantage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-2.htm
- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** "Gates" means places of trade and meeting. The Jews came to Jerusalem frequently from all parts, which increased her beauty and trade. New Tyre expects that more will come to her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 3 (many nations like waves)**
- **Many invaders over many centuries.** Ellicott says the prophet looks ahead through Tyre's whole future, past Nebuchadnezzar, with nation after nation striking her like waves on her rock. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **Guzik's list of the "waves":** Nebuchadnezzar (586–573 BC), Persia (about 525 BC), Alexander (332 BC), Antiochus III, Rome, and finally the Saracens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/
- **Tyre gets what she asked for.** Keil & Delitzsch say "many nations" is used because Tyre is hoping to attract more nations to itself in consequence of the destruction of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-2.htm

**v. 4 (bare rock)**
- **A pun on the name.** Guzik and Constable both note that "Tyre" means "rock," so making her a bare rock is wordplay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Fulfilled by Alexander, says Precept Austin.** He built a causeway out of mainland Tyre's rubble, and Thus Tyre was scraped bare as a rock, just as Ezekiel predicted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/fulfilled-bible-prophecy-destruction-of-tyre
- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** The rubble would be thrown into the sea, to make a road by which New Tyre in the island might be attacked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 5 (place for nets)**
- **A trader becomes plunder.** Constable says Tyre had once "spoiled" the nations through trade, and now she would become their spoil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Which part of Tyre is meant?** The commentators disagree.
  - JFB says the verse is plainly referring to New Tyre, the island city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
  - Haydock reports that St. Jerome explains this of New Tyre; Marsham of the Old. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 6 (mainland villages)**
- **"Daughters" means dependent towns.** Ellicott calls the "daughters in the field" a poetic way of naming Tyre's mainland dependencies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **"Then they will know that I am the LORD."** Constable reads this as saying that the fulfilment would convince many Tyrians that Yahweh was the true God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 7 (Nebuchadnezzar named)**
- **"From the north" and "king of kings."** Ellicott says "from the north" describes the route his armies took, even though Babylon actually lies south of Tyre. He is "king of kings" because many kings were his vassals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **First time named.** Guzik notes this is the first time Ezekiel names Nebuchadnezzar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/
- **Not a lucky guess.** JFB notes Shalmaneser, with all the might of the Assyrian empire, had failed in his siege of Tyre. Yet Nebuchadnezzar was to succeed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
- **A Catholic alternative.** Haydock cites Menochius, who allows that "king of kings" could mean Nebuchadnezzar or Alexander [the Great], who took Tyre. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**vv. 8–9 (the siege)**
- **Ordinary siege methods.** Ellicott says these are normal land-siege tactics, used against mainland Old Tyre. He thinks Nebuchadnezzar must also have found some way across to the island. The "shields" were a roof of shields to protect the besiegers. The word translated "axes" literally means "swords." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **What Nebuchadnezzar took.** Precept Austin says he broke down the walls of mainland Tyre (not the island). https://www.preceptaustin.org/fulfilled-bible-prophecy-destruction-of-tyre

**vv. 10–11 (the city entered; the pillars fall)**
- **The army got inside.** Ellicott says v. 10 implies Nebuchadnezzar's troops actually marched into the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **The "pillars."**
  - Ellicott thinks they are probably the gold and emerald pillars that the Greek historian Herodotus describes in Tyre's temple of Hercules. (same URL)
  - Constable allows either those temple pillars or Tyre's leading citizens. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Catholic reading.** Haydock (citing Calmet) says Old Tyre was taken by storm, but whether it was looted is uncertain, citing Ezekiel 29:18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 12 (from "he" to "they")** — the main point of debate in the chapter
- **The common evangelical reading: "they" includes Alexander.**
  - Guzik, Constable and Precept Austin all say the change from "he" (Nebuchadnezzar) to "they" points beyond him to later invaders. In 332 BC Alexander threw the rubble of mainland Tyre into the sea to build his causeway. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/fulfilled-bible-prophecy-destruction-of-tyre
  - Ellicott says much the same. He adds that the "spoil" means more what Tyre lost than what conquerors gained, because the Tyrians usually shipped their wealth away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
  - JFB calls Nebuchadnezzar's overthrow the first link in the long chain of evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch** do not bring in the "he/they" distinction. They simply describe the whole city being destroyed, so completely that they will sweep stones, wood, and rubbish into the sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-2.htm

**v. 13 (songs silenced)**
- **God acts directly here.** Ellicott says that in this verse God speaks of His own action, showing He ordered all these disasters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/26.htm
- **Cross-references.** Constable links the verse to Isaiah 23:16 and Revelation 18:22. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 14 ("You will never be rebuilt")** — interpretations really diverge here
- **The mainland city was never rebuilt.**
  - JFB says it was fulfilled as to the mainland Tyre under Nebuchadnezzar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
  - Clarke instead suspects the whole of this prophecy refers to Alexander. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/26-14.html
  - A Bible Hub article argues that modern Ṣūr overlays the former island, not the prophesied mainland. https://biblehub.com/q/Ezekiel_26_14_vs_Tyre_s_historical_fate.htm
- **"Rebuilt" means restored to former greatness.**
  - GotQuestions says *That* Tyre—the Tyre judged by God—will never be reconstituted or rebuilt. https://www.gotquestions.org/Tyre-rebuilt-prophecy.html
  - Constable quotes Stuart: the phrase means it will not go back to its former state, not that nothing would ever be built there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** He links the verse to Isaiah 23's seventy years, notes that New Tyre later thrived, and concludes all this must be understood of New Tyre. The old city never regained much splendour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **A more critical older view.** The Expositor's Bible (1887) reads Ezekiel 29:18 as showing that the historical event was not in accordance with the details of the earlier prophecy. It also says the destruction had not the finality which Ezekiel had anticipated. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/ezekiel/26-5.html
- **The Cambridge Bible's middle position.** Prophecies show God's moral rule over the world, though the form in which they clothe this exhibition may not be quite that given in history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-2.htm

**vv. 15–16 (the coastlands tremble; princes in mourning)**
- **Who trembles.** Constable says these are Tyre's colonies and dependent states around the Mediterranean, mourning their "mother city." He compares Job 2, Jonah 3 and Revelation 18:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **"Coastlands"/"isles."** Ellicott says the word means any sea-coast, not only islands. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Who the "princes" are.** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says they are not kings of the islands, but, according to Isaiah 23:8, the merchants presiding over the colonies of Tyre. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/ezekiel/26-5.html
- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** He names Tyrian colonies such as Leptis, Utica, Carthage,and Cadiz. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**vv. 17–18 (the lament)**
- **A funeral song.** Constable says it is written in the qinah (dirge) rhythm. He contrasts Tyre's gloating in v. 2 with these vassals' wiser fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **Hebrew detail.** JFB notes that "imposed terror" can be read as making every Tyrian feared. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
- **Tyre's terror.** Coffman connects the "terror" to Tyre as a slave-trading city. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 19 (the deep covers her)**
- **Two pictures mixed.** Constable says Ezekiel blends waves swamping a rock-city with a person going down to the grave. The "waters" are the waves of invaders from v. 3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html
- **A sinking ship.** Precept Austin: Poetically, Tyre, the important seafaring merchant city, would sink like a great ship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/fulfilled-bible-prophecy-destruction-of-tyre
- **Catholic reading (Haydock).** The "waters" are great armies. He adds that Jesus later went to that region (Matthew 15:21). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/ezekiel-26.html

**v. 20 (down to the Pit)**
- **The Pit is the world of the dead.** The Pulpit Commentary says The pit is sheol, Hades, the unseen world of the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-20.htm
- **A translation difference: whose "glory" or "splendour"?**
  - Older English Bibles read "I shall set glory in the land of the living." JFB takes this as God's glory in Judah, My presence symbolized by the Shekinah cloud, the antitype to which shall be Messiah. In other words, God's presence, ultimately fulfilled in Christ.
  - The BSB's "nor set in splendour" makes the splendour Tyre's. A Bible Hub exegetical note explains this reading, or an alternative reading presumably before LXX.
  - Both points: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-20.htm
- **Precept Austin** contrasts Tyre's end with glory in the land of the living. Life in the region would thrive after Tyre was forgotten. https://www.preceptaustin.org/fulfilled-bible-prophecy-destruction-of-tyre

**v. 21 (sought but never found)**
- **She stops being *that* Tyre.** JFB says the verse means not that presently there was to be no more a Tyre, but she was no more to be the Tyre that once she was. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-26.html
- **Gone from history.** Guzik says Tyre would leave the stage of history. Constable notes that only a small fishing village stands on the site today, and closes with 1 Corinthians 1:27–29, God shaming the strong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-26.html

---

**Themes across the chapter (for application)**
- **Selfishness that profits from others' ruin.** Matthew Henry treats it as a sin that easily besets us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-1.htm
- **The world gloating over the Church.** The Pulpit homilies use Tyre as a picture of this, and stress how insecure worldly greatness is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/26.htm
- **Judgment only, no hope offered.** JFB contrasts Ezekiel, who shows only the dark side for the nations, with Isaiah 23, which promises Tyre future blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/26-1.htm
- **Mercy in the delay.** Guzik and Constable note that Jesus later ministered around Tyre, and that Paul met believers there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-26/
